The plan for `vim.pos` and `vim.range` has been mostly implemented (big thanks to @ofseed @TheLeoP ). https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/25509 https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/38561

This tracks remaining work. See subissues also.
- [x] ~~do we need these fields?~~ [resolved](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/39867#issuecomment-4485570263)
  ```
  -- row_offset?: number
  -- col_offset?: number
  -- vcol?: number  -- virtual column
  -- vrow?: number  -- virtual row
  ```
- [ ] Do we need a `kind` field?
  ```
  vim.pos.Pos: {
    kind?: 'mark' | 'extmark' | 'cursor' | ...
  }
  ```
- [x] Test coverage could be stronger for the `to_inclusive_pos` logic and edge cases.
- [x] `Range.has` semantics: Tests only cover one case (`vim.range(0,0,0,4):has(vim.range(0,0,0,0))`). More edge cases would be valuable.
- [x] `Range.to_extmark/to_cursor` create temporary `vim.Pos` objects. This partially defeats the performance motivation? https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/39889
- [x] support `opts.win=0` to mean "current win"? https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/40087
- [ ]  docs: [callout integer indexing]
- [ ] Refactor old code to use `vim.pos` / `vim.range` 
     - [ ] [compare_position (vscode-neovim)](https://github.com/vscode-neovim/vscode-neovim/pull/1490/files#diff-356c71d28d1ad83654bec96ec39481938dd06e6589a05d781ed2ab028d9296b6R70-R84)
     - [ ] ?

comment_data.body: Sorry if this is noise but the docs could use some love, especially some examples would be nice. E.g. I would expect that `vim.pos.cursor()` will simply result in a `vim.pos.Pos` object that represents the current cursor position (like `getpos('.')`), but I can't even understand how to correctly call `vim.pos.cursor(...)` (probably a skill issue on my end tho)

> E.g. I would expect that `vim.pos.cursor()` will simply result in a `vim.pos.Pos` object that represents the current cursor position (like `getpos('.')`

yes we should consider that

> * [ ]  TODO: do we need these fields?
>   ```
>   -- row_offset?: number
>   -- col_offset?: number
>   -- vcol?: number  -- virtual column
>   -- vrow?: number  -- virtual row
>   ``` 
> * [ ]  Do we need a `kind` field?

I think we don't need them. Since we have already made `buf` a mandatory argument, I think the most appropriate meaning for the current `pos`/`range` is to represent a "position/range within a buffer." Our approach to any other type of range should be to convert them into a "position/range within a buffer," namely `vim.Pos`/`vim.Range`, or to convert out from such a range.

The benefit of binding positions and ranges to a buffer is that we can handle text encoding more accurately. Encoding affects more functionality than one might think; for example, when legally offsetting a position by one character to convert it between end-inclusive and end-exclusive, the buffer must be read to achieve this:
https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/f3bb21e71da09a357c0b05e53b4e11afdceb6621/runtime/lua/vim/range.lua#L148-L178

For visual positiontions, I think it is unlikely to be resolved by `vim.Pos`/`vim.Range`. To obtain a visual line in a buffer, we need to account for buffer encoding, calculate extmarks, and consider the statuscolumn/foldcolumn/signcolumn, etc. We should probably expose an API from C to handle this. Currently, we only have `vim.fn.winline`/`vim.fn.wincol` to get the cursor's visual position; we need an API to convert any buffer position into a visual position, such as `nvim_win_get_virtual_by_position(win, row, col)`, where `row` and `col` are 0-based buffer positions.

> get the cursor's visual position; we need an API to convert any buffer position into a visual position, such as `nvim_win_get_virtual_by_position`

`getregionpos()` and `nvim_win_text_height()` may be relevant

Not sure if this is directly related.

```lua
vim.lsp.util.make_position_params(win?: integer, position_encoding: "utf-16"|"utf-32"|"utf-8")
vim.lsp.util.make_range_params(win?: integer, position_encoding: "utf-16"|"utf-32"|"utf-8")
```

Both functions take a `win`, which is convenient until you need to create params for a specific position or range instead of the current cursor. It might make sense to overload them to also accept a `vim.pos`/`vim.range` in place of `win`, since `vim.pos` can already be constructed from either a window or a buffer and position.

Additionally, it can be useful for `vim.diagnostic.get()` to accept a `pos`/`range` for filtering instead of `lnum`.

I also noticed AI hallucinating `vim.range.selection(0)` a few times (similar to `vim.pos.cursor(0)`), and it actually seems like a good idea. It could return the current Visual selection range, or fallback to a cursor range (`start == end`) otherwise.
`getregionpos()` does that already, and `vim.pos` / `vim.range` are designed to produced forms accepted by such legacy functions.

> Not sure if this is directly related.
> 
> ```lua
> vim.lsp.util.make_position_params(win?: integer, position_encoding: "utf-16"|"utf-32"|"utf-8")
> vim.lsp.util.make_range_params(win?: integer, position_encoding: "utf-16"|"utf-32"|"utf-8")
> ```
> 
> Both functions take a `win`, which is convenient until you need to create params for a specific position or range instead of the current cursor. It might make sense to overload them to also accept a `vim.pos`/`vim.range` in place of `win`, since `vim.pos` can already be constructed from either a window or a buffer and position.

My original thought was planning to remove these two functions. Now that we have `vim.pos:to_lsp()`, they feel redundant. However, considering that a large number of users still seem to be using them, I decided to keep them and just reduce their usage in the current codebase.


To be more specific, most of their use cases can be directly replaced by `vim.pos.cursor(win):to_lsp()`.

>  most of their use cases can be directly replaced by `vim.pos.cursor(win):to_lsp()`.

good to know, but without those util functions it's still a bit clumsy?

make_position_params:

```lua
local win = 0
local params = {
  textDocument = vim.lsp.util.make_text_document_params(vim.api.nvim_win_get_buf(win)),
  position = vim.pos.cursor(win):to_lsp('utf-16'),
}
```

make_range_params:

```lua
local win = 0
local position = vim.pos.cursor(win):to_lsp('utf-16')
local params = {
  textDocument = vim.lsp.util.make_text_document_params(vim.api.nvim_win_get_buf(win)),
  range = { start = position, ['end'] = position },
}
```
`make_range_params` could also support the current Visual selection out of the box if `vim.range.selection/cursor()` won't be added.

> good to know, but without those util functions it's still a bit clumsy?

The issue is that the return types of these two functions are somewhat awkward. Currently, they return a table like this:

```lua
local params = {
  textDocument = …,
  position = …,
}
```

However, we often need to add other fields to `params`, for example:

```lua
local params = {
  -- same as above
  context = …,
}
```

This means we have to write code like this:

```lua
local params = make_position_params(…)
params.context = …
```

Therefore, I feel that this additional layer of wrapping is somewhat unnecessary.

Another issue is that it is inconsistent with the more commonly used `make_text_document_params`. We usually use that function like this:

```lua
local params = { textDocument = make_text_document_params(…) }
```

In contrast, `make_position_params` returns a value at a different structural level.

That said, these concerns are mostly aesthetic rather than practical. Since these functions may already have a large number of users, I ultimately decided not to remove them.

> `make_range_params` could also support the current Visual selection out of the box if `vim.range.selection/cursor()` won't be added.
> 

@drowning-cat `vim.range.mark(…):to_lsp()` is intended for exactly this purpose, because the vim convention is to use marks to represent a selection (`>` and `<` marks represent the two ends of a selection).

There was a `vim.range.cursor(…)` API briefly in the past, but it was eventually removed precisely because `vim.range.mark(…)` was considered a better replacement. 

It also handles some subtle edge cases. If you are interested, you can look up the previous PRs about this,I have gone into great detail about the reasoning behind.

> * [ ]  Do we need a `kind` field?
>   ```
>   vim.pos.Pos: {
>     kind?: 'mark' | 'extmark' | 'cursor' | ...
>   }
>   ```

This seems to be the last item on the checklist? Here is my take:

Since we describe `vim.Pos` as a "standard" position type, I don't think we need to make this distinction. The only purpose of such a field would be to indicate what other position type a `vim.Pos` was converted from, but we can achieve this through the `data` field I suggested before. Perhaps we could treat `pos.data` as the kind annotation by default, but I think we can add this later if it turns out to be necessary.

@ofseed

Thank you for the explanation :)

> Therefore, I feel that this additional layer of wrapping is somewhat unnecessary.

I initially thought this API was meant to either abstract over request structure changes or, in the case of `make_range_params`, automatically handle the current visual selection. But since it only saves a few lines of code, it might indeed be unnecessary.

> There was a `vim.range.cursor(…)` API briefly in the past, but it was eventually removed precisely because `vim.range.mark(…)` was considered a better replacement.

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/9c5afe660667537f876d11c0486bedd7eb363e61/runtime/lua/vim/range.lua#L334-L343

For me, the main issue with this approach is that you have to leave visual mode before you can get the selected range. `getregionpos()` can be used instead, but I feel like there might be a simple way to get the current visual selection as a range to send to the LSP server (e.g. via `vim.lsp.util`).

I'm not very familiar with the LSP stuff, but the fact that ranges are sent to the server implies that sending the current visual selection is a fairly common use case.

For example, here's one place where it could be useful:

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/2f9ef98a331959ea6fdb12337be5337df561ac06/runtime/lua/vim/lsp/buf.lua#L1353

https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/2f9ef98a331959ea6fdb12337be5337df561ac06/runtime/lua/vim/lsp/buf.lua#L542-L573

Utility example:

```lua
---@return vim.Range
local get_cursor_range = function(win)
  return vim.api.nvim_win_call(win, function()
    local v_mode = string.match(vim.api.nvim_get_mode().mode, "[Vv\22]")
    local regpos = vim.fn.getregionpos(vim.fn.getpos("v"), vim.fn.getpos("."), {
      type = v_mode == "V" and "V" or "v",
      exclusive = false,
    })
    local rs, re = regpos[1][1], regpos[#regpos][2]
    return vim.range(0, rs[2] - 1, rs[3] - 1, re[2] - 1, re[3] - (v_mode and 0 or 1))
  end)
end
```

Should range and position also support `:is_valid()` to check whether they are applicable to the buffer, or is it too much? Check that the buffer is valid and that the position or range is within its boundaries.
